opus-5.5.text:
Computational irreducibility is real, but I think people draw the wrong conclusion from it. Wolfram's point is that for many systems there's no shortcut: to know what happens at step a million, you have to run all million steps. Some people hear that and conclude that prediction is hopeless and intelligence is overrated. I think that's a big mistake.

First, irreducibility is a statement about exact prediction of every detail. Intelligence almost never needs that. I don't need to simulate every molecule in this room to know that if I drop my cup, it falls. The world has enormous pockets of reducibility: regularities, symmetries, conserved quantities, and statistical laws that emerge at higher levels. Thermodynamics is the classic example. The microdynamics of a gas may be irreducible, yet pressure and temperature are perfectly predictable. A big part of what learning *is* is finding those pockets, the coarse-grained variables where the world becomes compressible. If the world weren't largely reducible at the levels we care about, neither we nor any AI could exist as intelligent agents, because there'd be nothing to learn.

Second, where irreducibility genuinely bites, the right response isn't to give up on prediction. It's to change how you act. You predict probabilistically instead of deterministically. You plan over shorter horizons and replan as information comes in. You hedge, you take actions that keep options open, you act to *find out* rather than assuming you already know. That's what good decision-making under uncertainty looks like, and it's what people do in poker, business, and war. Being robust beats being precisely right about an unknowable future.

Third, and this is underappreciated: an agent doesn't just predict the world, it shapes it. If a system is hard to predict, often you can intervene to make it more predictable. That's what engineering is. We build bridges and circuits precisely so their behavior is reducible. An AI that understands this will partly control its environment rather than only forecast it.

And then there's the practical side. Sometimes simulation really is the only way, and that's fine. You run the simulation, you use Monte Carlo, you let the system play out in a sandbox. Irreducible doesn't mean incomputable; it just means no free lunch. My view of the master algorithm is something that combines all of these: learning compressible structure where it exists, reasoning probabilistically where it doesn't, and simulating when there's no shortcut, while knowing which situation you're in. That meta-knowledge, knowing when you can shortcut and when you can't, may be the most important part.

So computational irreducibility is a useful reminder of humility, but it's not a ceiling on AI. Humans live in an irreducible universe too, and we've done pretty well by exploiting the parts that aren't.

r001.rationale: It says irreducible systems can still be simulated step by step, but may have no shortcut, distinguishing computability in principle from practical computational cost.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says the world has “enormous pockets of reducibility” amid irreducible systems.

r003.rationale: It does not characterize evolution as an accumulation of computationally reducible pieces.

r004.rationale: It recommends replanning as information comes in, which communicates updating predictions in response to observations.

r005.rationale: It discusses probabilistic prediction and robust action, but does not state that predictions need only be accurate enough to support control.

r006.rationale: It advocates intervening to make systems more predictable and says an AI can partly control its environment.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the first thing I'd say is that computational irreducibility is real, but it's much less of a problem than people like Stephen Wolfram make it out to be. Yes, there are systems where the only way to find out what happens is to run them step by step, and no shortcut exists. Cellular automata, chaotic dynamics, that kind of thing. But the striking fact about the world we actually live in, and the reason science works at all, is that most of what we care about is highly reducible. The world is compressible. That's the whole premise of machine learning. If the world weren't full of regularities, learning would be impossible, and so would intelligence, and so would we.

So the way I'd put it is this. The goal of an intelligent agent is not to predict everything. It's to predict what matters, at the level of abstraction where the prediction is tractable and useful. You don't need to simulate every molecule of air to predict that it's going to rain tomorrow. You don't need to predict the exact trajectory of every car to drive safely. Evolution figured this out long before we did. Animals operate in a wildly irreducible world and they do fine, because they learned the regularities that are relevant to survival and they ignore the rest.

And the second part of your question is actually the more important one, which is acting. People tend to think of AI as prediction followed by action, but the two are deeply intertwined. When you can't predict, you act in ways that make prediction unnecessary. You build in slack. You make reversible decisions. You keep options open. You sense and respond instead of planning everything out in advance. This is what control theory and reinforcement learning are about, fundamentally. The thermostat doesn't have a model of the weather. It has a feedback loop. A lot of intelligence is about choosing the policy that is robust to your own ignorance, rather than trying to eliminate the ignorance.

There's also a very practical point here, which is that irreducibility is often an argument for learning as opposed to hand-engineering. If you can't derive the behavior of a system from first principles in less time than it takes to just run it, then the thing to do is observe it and learn a model. That model will be approximate, and in a sense it's cheating, because it's compressing something that in principle can't be compressed. But approximate is fine. Most of the time what you need is a model that's right often enough, at the granularity that matters, with calibrated uncertainty where it isn't.

And I'd add one thing about the current generation of systems. Large language models are enormous engines of compression, and in a way that's exactly what you want in an irreducible world. They're finding the regularities. But they're not very good at knowing where their compression breaks down, and that's where the real work is. An AI that handles irreducibility well is one that knows the boundary between what it can predict and what it can't, and switches strategies at that boundary. It plans where planning works, it experiments where it doesn't, and it knows the difference. That, to me, is much closer to what we mean by intelligence than any amount of raw predictive power.

r001.rationale: It describes systems with no shortcut and models learned by observation, but does not clearly distinguish predictability in principle from computational feasibility in practice.

r002.rationale: It says the world is mostly reducible and that some systems are irreducible, but does not state that an irreducible universe can contain reducible subsystems.

r003.rationale: It says evolution led animals to learn relevant regularities, but does not characterize evolution as accumulating computationally reducible pieces.

r004.rationale: It mentions feedback and sensing and responding, but does not advocate continually recalibrating predictions with incoming observations.

r005.rationale: It says a model need only be right often enough and at the granularity that matters, and frames useful prediction as supporting an agent's decisions and actions.

r006.rationale: It advocates robust actions that make prediction unnecessary, such as keeping options open and using feedback, rather than controlling the world to make it more predictable.

astra-6.text:
Well, computational irreducibility means that, for some processes, there’s no shortcut to finding out what happens—you have to let the process run. But that doesn’t mean that nothing useful can be predicted. You may not be able to predict the exact state of a system, yet you can predict properties of it that matter for your decision.

So I think the first question for AI is: what do you actually need to know? You don’t need to predict every molecule in the atmosphere to decide whether to take an umbrella. You need a prediction at the right level of abstraction, with enough accuracy to guide that action.

And acting in the world isn’t just making one prediction and committing to it forever. You act, you observe what happens, and you revise. Where prediction is expensive or unreliable, you want feedback, experiments, and actions that work reasonably well across different possible outcomes.

The mistake would be to treat computational irreducibility either as something intelligence can magically overcome or as a reason to give up on prediction. It’s a constraint. The interesting problem is how much useful intelligence you can build within that constraint.

r001.rationale: It describes irreducible processes as having no shortcut and requiring the process to run, distinguishing computational limits from useful predictions that remain possible.

r002.rationale: It does not state that an irreducible universe can contain computationally reducible subsystems.

r003.rationale: It says nothing about evolution accumulating computationally reducible pieces.

r004.rationale: It advocates acting, observing outcomes, and revising predictions.

r005.rationale: It says predictions need enough accuracy to guide an action.

r006.rationale: It recommends feedback, experiments, and robust actions, but does not advocate controlling the world to make it more predictable.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first thing is to distinguish predicting everything from predicting what matters. Even if the only way to know the exact state of a system a thousand steps from now is to run it for a thousand steps, that doesn’t mean there’s nothing useful you can say about it. You may still be able to predict its large-scale behavior, or identify actions that work across a range of possible outcomes.

For an AI, the question is: what do I need to know to make this decision? You don’t need to predict every other driver’s trajectory all the way home to drive a car. You need a model that’s good enough over the relevant horizon, and then you observe what happens and update.

So I would treat computational irreducibility as a constraint on prediction, not as a reason to give up on intelligence. Use approximations, simulate where it’s worth the cost, represent uncertainty, and keep learning as you act. Sometimes the intelligent thing is to spend more computation. Sometimes it’s to take a small, reversible action and let the world give you the information.

r001.rationale: It contrasts exact-state prediction requiring a long simulation with useful approximate predictions that are feasible for decisions.

r002.rationale: It does not state that a computationally irreducible universe can contain computationally reducible subsystems.

r003.rationale: It does not characterize evolution as accumulating computationally reducible pieces.

r004.rationale: It says to observe what happens, update the model, and keep learning while acting.

r005.rationale: It says the model only needs to be good enough for the decision over the relevant horizon.

r006.rationale: It suggests reversible actions to gain information, but does not advocate controlling the world to make it more predictable.
